title: PKK Peace Law Enters Force, Black Sea Transits Resume After Strait Disruption, Mecca Pact Tested by Houthi Strike on Saudi Refinery
subhead: Turkey's 'terror-free Turkey' law passed parliament 468-88, creating a legal framework for PKK disbandment — but the group warns Ocalan's exclusion could make it a dead letter. Black Sea shipping transits resumed after unexplained delays, while Kazakhstan turned to the BTC pipeline as an alternative to Russian routes. The Mecca defense pact faced its first test when Houthi drones hit a Saudi refinery and no mutual defense response followed.

sections.heading: PKK Peace Law Passes Parliament 468-88, But Ocalan Question Lingers
sections.body:
Turkey's parliament passed the 'Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Unity Act' — dubbed the 'terror-free Turkey law' — by 468 votes to 88 with six abstentions after 12 hours of debate broadcast live on TRT. The legislation, backed by the AKP, MHP, and pro-Kurdish DEM Party, creates a legal framework for the disbandment of the PKK and the reintegration of its fighters, according to Reuters and France 24.

The law suspends prosecutions and prison sentences for eligible offenses for between five and 10 years, with permanent closure if no new crimes are committed. It is expected to lead to the release of approximately 3,500 PKK-linked detainees in an initial phase — roughly a third of those held in Turkish prisons, lawmakers said. Those convicted of serious crimes such as intentional murder are excluded, France 24 reported.

Crucially, the text makes no mention of Abdullah Ocalan, the PKK founder imprisoned on Imrali island since 1999. Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz told CNN Turk that Ocalan's case 'does not fall within the scope of this law' but said he would be 'in a position to contribute to the peace process.' The PKK leadership warned on Sunday that excluding Ocalan would render many of the law's provisions a 'dead letter,' France 24 reported.

Nationalist opposition Iyi Party lawmaker Turhan Comez challenged the bill during debate: 'How can you negotiate with terrorists? ... You said they would be laying down their weapons unconditionally,' he said. DEM MP Ceylan Akca called the vote 'crossing a historic threshold' and 'the first step of a long walk towards absolute and authentic equality.'
sections.whyItMatters: The 468-88 vote gives the peace process its legislative backbone — but the Ocalan gap is the fault line. If the PKK concludes the law is insufficient without his release, the disbandment process stalls at the starting line. The government has bet that momentum and the broad parliamentary coalition will carry the process forward regardless.

sections.heading: Black Sea Transits Resume After Unexplained Delays
sections.body:
Turkey has resumed the transit of ships through its straits en route to the Black Sea following unexplained delays for some vessels, Bloomberg reported on Sunday. The oil tanker Aegean Dream entered the Dardanelles Strait after waiting in the area since Thursday, listing the Caspian Pipeline Consortium terminal in Novorossiysk, Russia as its destination. The container ship Mehmet Kahveci A also passed through, also bound for Novorossiysk.

Turkey's General Directorate of Coastal Safety had recently informed some vessels bound for Russian and Ukrainian ports that it was not issuing transit permits, without disclosing the reason. The Ministry of Transport and Infrastructure did not respond to Bloomberg's inquiry on Sunday.

Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said in an overnight interview with Anadolu Agency that Turkey has appealed to both Russia and Ukraine to declare a 'moratorium' on military operations in the Black Sea, adding: 'We have developed a series of measures on this issue, which we have presented to our president. We are now putting them into practice.'

A US official told Bloomberg that Ukraine had agreed to help ensure safe passage for some non-Russian oil tankers. The delays appeared linked to Turkish concerns about drone attacks on merchant shipping in the Black Sea, some of which targeted Turkish-owned or Turkish-flagged vessels.
sections.whyItMatters: The brief suspension and resumption of strait transits was a calibrated signal: Ankara showed it can restrict Black Sea access under the Montreux Convention, then eased once it extracted Ukrainian cooperation on safe passage. The Fidan moratorium proposal, if it gains traction, could reshape Black Sea commercial logistics — and Turkey's role as gatekeeper.

sections.heading: Kazakhstan Turns to BTC Pipeline as Ukrainian Drones Squeeze Russian Routes
sections.body:
Kazakhstan's Ministry of Energy said on Monday it is considering re-routing crude oil exports through the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan (BTC) pipeline, via Caspian Sea shipments through Azerbaijan, and through the Baku-Supsa route, as Ukrainian drone attacks repeatedly shut down the Caspian Pipeline Consortium terminal at Novorossiysk, Oilprice.com reported.

In July alone, CPC flows were suspended on three separate occasions due to drone strikes. The latest week-long shutdown removed more than 1 million barrels per day of Kazakh production from the market. CPC handles most of Kazakhstan's crude exports from its giant Tengiz, Kashagan, and Karachaganak fields, operated by Chevron, ExxonMobil, Shell, and Eni.

Kazakhstan is also exploring boosting supply eastward via pipeline to China. But BTC — which terminates at Turkey's Mediterranean port of Ceyhan — represents the most viable large-scale alternative, even though its capacity is significantly smaller than CPC's 1.5 million bpd throughput.
sections.whyItMatters: Every disruption to Novorossiysk makes Ceyhan more attractive as an alternative export route. If Kazakhstan begins routing meaningful volumes through BTC, Turkey gains revenue, leverage, and strategic relevance as an energy corridor — at Russia's expense.

sections.heading: Mecca Pact's First Test: Houthi Strike on Saudi Refinery Draws No Mutual Defense Response
sections.body:
Two days after Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, Houthi forces attacked Saudi Aramco's Jazan refinery with a drone. The Saudi Energy Ministry confirmed a fire was extinguished with no casualties, Reuters reported. Neither Turkey nor Pakistan invoked the pact's mutual defense clause or issued a military response.

The silence was significant. Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has described the pact's collective defense provision as 'technically the same as NATO's Article 5,' and officials from all three countries have insisted it is not directed against any particular state. A permanent secretariat is to be established in Saudi Arabia with regular coordination among foreign and defense officials, The Media Line reported.

Analysts frame the pact differently depending on their vantage point. Blue Water Strategy's Cyril Widdershoven told The Media Line that Riyadh is building 'strategic redundancy' — maintaining the US relationship for high-end weapons and intelligence while adding Turkey for 'operational experience, defense technology, and geopolitical reach' and Pakistan for workforce and training. Israeli Diaspora Affairs Minister Amichai Chikli called the pact a 'very dangerous and very troubling development' and advocated deepening ties with Greece, Cyprus, and the UAE.

Iran dismissed the pact as a 'paper agreement' and a 'paper tiger,' arguing that Saudi Arabia has not taken action against any of the aggressors attacking its territory, according to the Jerusalem Post and Moneycontrol.
sections.whyItMatters: The Jazan strike was the pact's first real-world test — and the response was consultation, not action. That is likely the correct reading: the Mecca pact is an insurance policy and a deterrent signal, not an immediate-response mechanism. But the gap between Fidan's Article 5 framing and the actual response to an attack on Saudi territory will not be lost on regional adversaries.

sections.heading: Washington Post Reveals Trump's Secret Departure From Ankara Amid Iran Assassination Threat
sections.body:
The Washington Post reported on Sunday that President Donald Trump was secretly transported out of Turkey on an alternate military aircraft during last month's NATO summit, after US intelligence identified an Iranian assassination threat. The White House had publicly stated Trump was aboard Air Force One, but he was instead moved to a C-32A military jet — the same type used by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth — via an airport catering truck used to conceal his movement on the tarmac.

Members of the White House press corps aboard Air Force One were unaware of the switch, and a pool reporter had noted that window shades were ordered closed during departure. Trump arrived at RAF Mildenhall in England on the alternate aircraft before transferring back to the presidential plane for the transatlantic leg, USA Today reported.

White House Communications Director Steven Cheung confirmed the deception: 'As the President has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal — including distraction and misdirection — to address those threats.'

The revelation highlights the security environment in Ankara during the NATO summit and raises questions about what Turkish intelligence knew about the Iranian threat and whether Ankara's security guarantees for the summit were considered sufficient by Washington.
sections.whyItMatters: The fact that the US president felt compelled to use a decoy aircraft and a catering truck to leave Turkey speaks volumes about the security assessment of Ankara during the NATO summit. It also underscores the intensity of the Iran threat environment that continues to shape regional calculations.

sections.heading: Hormuz Reopening Conditions Hardening as Oil Climbs 5%
sections.body:
Oil prices settled 5% higher on Monday after Iran and the United States traded compensation demands, dimming prospects for a swift reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi reiterated that the strait would only reopen once the US lifts sanctions and pays reparations, while Trump demanded Iran compensate American families for attacks linked to Iranian-backed groups, Reuters and AOL reported.

Brent crude rose above $90 a barrel on the exchange. An Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson said Iranians had 'shown they are professional chess players,' rejecting Trump's framing of American naval control over Hormuz, MSN reported.

For Turkey, the Hormuz standoff continues to cut both ways: higher oil prices feed into domestic inflation (still at 31.75% annually), but the extended closure maintains the strategic premium on BTC and other overland routes through Turkish territory. The longer Iran holds out, the more Ankara benefits from alternative corridor demand — and the more it risks if the strait suddenly reopens.
sections.whyItMatters: The widening gap between Iranian and American demands suggests Hormuz will not reopen quickly. For Turkey, this is a double-edged sword: expensive energy keeps inflation elevated, but transit route relevance stays high. The strategic calculus shifts the moment a deal is struck.

bottomLine: Monday's biggest development was the passage of the PKK peace law by a 468-88 margin — the first legislative milestone in a process that began with Ocalan's disarmament call 18 months ago. But the law's silence on Ocalan's fate is the fault line that could determine whether the process succeeds or stalls. Black Sea transits resumed after Turkey briefly flexed its Montreux Convention authority, extracting Ukrainian cooperation on safe passage before easing restrictions. Kazakhstan's pivot toward the BTC pipeline is a direct consequence of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian export infrastructure — and a quiet gain for Turkey's strategic position as an energy corridor. The Mecca defense pact's first real test, a Houthi strike on a Saudi refinery, produced consultations rather than action — revealing the gap between Fidan's Article 5 rhetoric and the pact's operational reality.
sources: Reuters, France 24, Al-Monitor, Bloomberg, Oilprice.com, The Media Line, USA Today, Washington Post, New York Times, Anadolu Agency, AP, Jerusalem Post, Moneycontrol, Middle East Eye, Israel National News, MSN, CPA (APA Azerbaijan)
